strengths: Well-motivated and timely negative result: the paper rigorously stress-tests the widely-repeated claim that FNOs (and mesh-invariant MLOs generally) enable zero-shot super-resolution, which is important for the scientific ML community.

Excellent problem decomposition: separating multi-resolution inference into (i) resolution interpolation (varying sampling rate) and (ii) information extrapolation (varying frequency content) is a clean, insightful framing that makes the failure modes of MLOs precisely diagnosable, supported by spectral analysis of residuals and clear aliasing visualizations (Figs. 1, 3-5).

Comprehensive and well-controlled experiments: three standard PDE datasets (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) at multiple resolutions, grid-searched hyperparameters, controlled low-pass filtering, ablation over FNO max modes (Appendix I), and systematic evaluation of two previously proposed corrective approaches (physics-informed losses of PINO, and band-limited learning via CNO and CROP), with the useful conclusion that neither fixes the core OOD issue.

Practically useful contribution: the multi-resolution training protocol includes a thoughtful cost-benefit analysis (Pareto tradeoff between average data size and multi-resolution test loss in Fig. 9), showing mostly-low-resolution data suffices, which is actionable guidance for practitioners.
Generally clear writing, honest reporting (e.g., CNO non-convergence on Burgers noted), thorough appendices, and code/implementation details that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central finding: that ML models fail to predict frequencies not seen in training is expected (and arguably information-theoretically inevitable); several prior works already critique discretization-invariance of neural operators (e.g., Gao et al., 2025, cited in the paper; Bartolucci et al., 2023; Krishnapriyan et al., 2021). The paper's main claim amounts to a systematic empirical confirmation of a largely anticipated failure mode.

The proposed solution (multi-resolution training, i.e., training on mixed-resolution data) is straightforward and closely builds on existing multi-resolution/active-learning approaches (Li et al., 2024a), which limits the methodological contribution; no theoretically grounded or architecturally novel remedy is offered.

Breadth of the negative claim is narrower than the title suggests: the core evaluation is on FNO only; other mesh-invariant operators (DeepONet, GNO, U-NO, TFNO variants) are discussed in related work but not tested, yet conclusions are phrased about 'MLOs' generally.

Some experimental details weaken interpretability: Navier-Stokes losses of 2E+10/2E+11 in Fig. 16 indicate training failures rather than pure generalization failure; hyperparameters were tuned only at one resolution per dataset and reused elsewhere; no error bars or seeds reported.

No analytical or theoretical treatment of when/why aliasing occurs (e.g., relation to FNO mode truncation and pointwise nonlinearities), leaving the paper purely empirical; some figures (Figs. 8, 28-30) are dense and hard to parse.

The evaluation of corrective methods could be seen as slightly unfavorable: physics-loss weighting is tuned with a small grid, and the CROP/CNO baselines, while appropriately chosen, are compared under conditions favoring full-spectrum modeling.

strengths: The decomposition of multi-resolution inference into two distinct capabilities—resolution interpolation and information extrapolation—is a clean, well-motivated framing that makes the failure modes of neural operators easier to diagnose.

The empirical study is broad in scope: three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes), multiple training resolutions, low-pass filter sweeps, and extensive appendices, with spectral analysis providing mechanistic insight into aliasing.
The paper evaluates two previously proposed corrective approaches (physics-informed losses and band-limited learning such as CNO/CROP) rather than only pointing out failures, which adds value.

The proposed multi-resolution training protocol is simple, practical, and the Pareto analysis of data cost vs. test loss (e.g., using mostly cheap low-resolution data with small amounts of high-resolution data) offers actionable guidance for practitioners.
The max-modes ablation in Appendix I is a useful contribution that disentangles an FNO-specific design choice from the general failure mode.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core finding—that neural operators fail to generalize across discretizations and exhibit aliasing—is largely already established in prior work that the authors themselves cite (e.g., Gao et al., ICLR 2025 on discretization mismatch errors; Brandstetter et al. on multi-scale message passing; Bartolucci et al. on alias-free operator learning). The paper is primarily a confirmatory empirical study with a stronger 'false promise' framing than genuinely new insight.

Overgeneralized conclusions from a single architecture: despite claims about 'MLOs' in general, essentially all main experiments use the FNO. DeepONet, GNO, U-NO, TFNO, and other mesh-invariant operators are never evaluated, yet the abstract and conclusion claim MLOs 'are not able to perform accurate inference' broadly. This mismatch between evidence and claims is significant.

Internal inconsistency in results presentation: the caption of Fig. 26 states CNO/CROP 'incur lower losses across resolutions compared to both FNO and multi-resolution training,' which appears to contradict the claims in Sec. 4.2 and Appendix F that multi-resolution training outperforms band-limited methods. This undermines confidence in the correctness of the reported results and their interpretation.

The negative result on physics-informed constraints may conflate known optimization difficulties of PINN-style losses with their inability to enable multi-resolution generalization; the weight sweep (w in {0.1, 0.25, 0.5}) and limited tuning are thin support for the strong conclusion drawn.

The proposed multi-resolution training is a straightforward data-mixture strategy whose efficacy is already suggested by prior multi-resolution/active-learning work (Li et al., 2024a); the paper provides no theory, no principled selection rule for resolution ratios ('optimizing the ratios remains an exciting future direction'), and no comparison against simpler baselines such as training exclusively on downsampled/high-res data or inference-time low-pass filtering followed by interpolation.

Reproducibility concerns: the 'Code:' placeholder on page 1 is empty, no discussion of random seeds, variance across runs, or statistical significance is provided for headline claims, and some results (e.g., CNO failing to converge on Burgers in Fig. 25) hint at implementation/tuning fragility.

Figures are often dense and hard to read (e.g., Figs. 8, 28-30), and key conclusions rest on visually judged spectral divergence rather than quantitative metrics with uncertainty, making the strength of claims like 'fail to do both tasks in a zero-shot manner' harder to verify.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question for scientific ML: whether the widely-repeated 'zero-shot super-resolution' claim for FNOs/neural operators actually holds. A rigorous, well-supported negative result here has real value for practitioners and for calibrating community expectations.

The decomposition of multi-resolution inference into two axes (resolution interpolation vs. frequency information extrapolation) is a clean, useful conceptual framing that makes the empirical study systematic rather than anecdotal.

The evaluation is comprehensive: three standard PDE datasets (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) from PDEBench, multiple resolutions and filter limits per dataset, hyperparameter grid searches, spectral (energy spectrum) analysis of residuals rather than only MSE, and additional ablations on max modes (Appendix I).

The study of corrective methods is valuable: it tests physics-informed constraints (Li et al., 2024b) and band-limited learning (CNO, CROP) and gives a coherent explanation for why neither works (the task is fundamentally OOD), rather than just reporting failure.

The proposed multi-resolution training protocol is practical and the cost-vs-loss tradeoff analysis (Fig. 9, Fig. 31) is a genuinely useful contribution: showing that mostly low-resolution data with a small amount of high-resolution data suffices has direct implications for data-generation budgeting.
The paper is generally well written, with clear motivating figures (Fig. 1-3) and honest framing of limitations and future work.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central finding. The skepticism toward FNO zero-shot super-resolution is not new: Tran et al. (2021) already questioned discretization generalization, and Gao et al. (2025, ICLR) explicitly studied discretization mismatch errors in neural operators. The paper's main empirical conclusions are largely confirmatory of what OOD-generalization reasoning would predict, which weakens the surprise/impact of the headline claim ('false promise').

The proposed remedy (multi-resolution training, i.e., training on data matching the test distribution) is straightforward and expected; the main insight is essentially 'include test-distribution data in training,' and the ratio tuning is a heuristic rather than a principled method. Active-learning style selection is deferred to future work.

Although the abstract/intro target 'machine-learned operators' broadly, the deep analysis is confined to FNO (with CNO/CROP in a supporting role). Generalizing conclusions to 'MLOs' as a class without testing, e.g., DeepONet, GNO, or U-NO, is an overreach; the paper itself lists these as mesh-invariant alternatives in Related Work.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported; conclusions like 'losses vary by 1x, 2x, 10x' (Fig. 16) would be more convincing with variance quantification, especially given known training instability of FNOs.

The physics-loss comparison may conflate two issues: physics constraints are known to be hard to optimize in general (the paper cites this), so their failure to fix multi-resolution inference does not strongly test the specific claim in Li et al. (2024b); the tuning range w in {0.1, 0.25, 0.5} may not cover configurations where the physics term helps.

Some experimental details are under-specified in the main text (e.g., exact dataset sizes per resolution, how train/test splits are constructed across resolutions, whether the same samples are used at different resolutions), which matters for interpreting the interpolation vs. extrapolation experiments; the code link on page 1 is an empty placeholder ('Code:'), weakening reproducibility as submitted.

Writing/polish issues: several typos ('constrains', 'interpolations', 'Freqeuncy', 'avaliable'), Eq. (2) for aliasing is presented without derivation or discussion of its assumptions, and some figures (e.g., Figs. 8, 28-30) are dense and hard to parse, burying key results in appendices.

The claim that multi-resolution training 'overcomes aliasing' is somewhat stronger than the evidence: the method improves fit across trained resolutions, but behavior at resolutions not represented in training is not fully characterized.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper carefully decomposes 'zero-shot multi-resolution inference' into two distinct capabilities (resolution interpolation and frequency information extrapolation), which makes the failure modes of MLOs precise and interpretable rather than anecdotal.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three standard PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) at a wide range of resolutions, with hyperparameter grid searches, spectral diagnostics (energy spectra and normalized residuals), and loss heatmaps that make the aliasing phenomenon convincing.

The paper does not stop at a negative result: it critically evaluates two previously proposed corrective approaches (physics-informed optimization constraints and band-limited learning via CNO/CROP) and provides concrete evidence that neither resolves the core issue, which is a valuable service to the community given the popularity of these claims.

The proposed multi-resolution training is simple, practical, and well-analyzed: the paper profiles the cost-quality tradeoff (data size vs. test loss Pareto front, memory and wall-clock savings of 56-98%), showing that mostly low-resolution data suffices, which increases practical adoption potential.

Exceptional appendix rigor: sensitivity analysis over random seeds, ablations over FNO max-modes, anti-aliasing activations, downsampling strategies (strided, pooling, bilinear), extension to DeepONet, and reproduction across six computing architectures — this level of robustness checking is well above average.
Strong reproducibility statement with code promised, detailed implementation configurations, and explicit acknowledgment of hardware/software variability.

Clear, honest framing of the limitations of zero-shot claims, which is timely and has real significance for practitioners relying on resolution invariance in MLOs (e.g., adaptive mesh refinement workflows).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core negative finding — that neural networks fail on out-of-distribution inputs, and that changing resolution is effectively OOD — is largely predictable from existing ML generalization theory, and multi-resolution/multi-fidelity training is already established (Li et al. 2024a, Rowbottom, Lanthaler, etc.). The paper is primarily a rigorous empirical confirmation rather than a new method or theory.

The main text focuses almost exclusively on FNO, with other architectures (DeepONet, CNO) relegated to appendices; the sweeping title and abstract claims about 'machine-learned operators' broadly would be better supported by more prominent multi-architecture results (e.g., graph-based or transformer-based operators are absent).

The proposed remedy (multi-resolution training) is a straightforward data-mixing recipe with limited analysis of why it works (no theoretical grounding) and no automated or principled strategy for choosing ratios, which the authors themselves defer to future work.

Some experimental conclusions rely on qualitative inspection of spectra; quantitative aggregate metrics (e.g., AUC of residual spectra or per-frequency error) are inconsistently reported in the main text, making some comparisons harder to assess at a glance.

The physics-informed loss evaluation, while thorough, may understate the potential of physics constraints given known optimization difficulties; the paper's conclusion that physics constraints 'do not enable' multi-resolution generalization could be seen as somewhat strong relative to the tuning effort invested.

Significance, while real for the SciML community, is moderate: the paper refines expectations for a specific class of architectures and tasks rather than opening a new research direction, and the practical impact depends on adoption of multi-resolution training which is a known technique.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important question: whether machine-learned operators (MLOs) can perform zero-shot super-/sub-resolution inference, a claim that has been made in the FNO literature and relied upon in practice.

The decomposition of multi-resolution inference into two distinct capabilities (resolution interpolation under fixed frequency content, and information extrapolation under fixed sampling rate) is a clean and useful experimental design, and the signal-processing/aliasing framing is pedagogically clear.

The empirical study is broad: three standard PDE datasets, multiple resolutions, additional architectures (CNO, CROP, DeepONet) and corrective strategies (physics-informed losses, band-limited learning, anti-alias activations, max-modes ablation) examined largely in the appendix, plus multi-seed sensitivity checks and down-sampling-strategy ablations.

The negative results on physics-informed constraints and band-limited methods (they neither extrapolate frequency content nor interpolate across resolutions) are informative and go beyond a simple 'FNO fails' statement.
Considerable reproducibility effort is described (hyperparameter grids, hardware portability tests across six computing architectures, detailed appendices).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core finding. That neural operators trained at one resolution fail to generalize to other resolutions and exhibit aliasing is largely known and has been reported in prior work that the paper itself cites (e.g., the discretization-invariance literature, the CNO paper, Gao et al. 2025). The paper's contribution is mostly a careful re-documentation of a known failure mode with a new framing, which is insufficient for a top-tier venue.

The proposed remedy, multi-resolution training, is essentially standard data mixing across resolutions and is explicitly acknowledged as previously proposed (Li et al. 2024a, Rowbottom et al., George et al., Tang et al., Lyu et al., Ma et al., Lanthaler et al.). The only new element is an empirical study of data-ratio trade-offs, which is heuristic and without analysis or principled guidance for choosing ratios.

There is no theoretical analysis of why aliasing/interpolation failure occurs or when multi-resolution training should help; all conclusions are purely empirical observations from energy spectra, making the paper feel more like a benchmark report than a research contribution.

Overly broad claims from limited evidence: the abstract and framing indict 'MLOs' generally, but the main-text analysis centers on FNO, with DeepONet and CNO/CROP relegated to appendices; other important operator families (mesh-invariant variants, GNOs, transformer-based operators) are not evaluated.

Experiments are restricted to three standard PDEBench-style datasets (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes); no realistic or higher-dimensional/multi-scale scenarios, which would be the settings where multi-resolution inference actually matters.

Several presentation problems reduce clarity: Figures 8 and 28-30 are dense and hard to parse; the main text reports loss trade-offs (e.g., Fig. 9) without precise numbers; some text-figure mismatches (e.g., Navier-Stokes loss values '2.8 vs 3.3'); and the 'Code:' field in the paper is empty — the reproducibility statement only promises a link upon acceptance, so reproducibility cannot be verified.

The paper is written as a rebuttal ('false promise') of specific claims in prior work, but the evaluation protocol (low-pass filtering, strided downsampling) introduces its own distribution shifts, and the boundary between 'resolution shift' and 'frequency content shift' is manipulated by the authors' data construction rather than arising naturally; this weakens the strength of the central indictment.

The main positive result (multi-resolution training with mostly low-resolution data) shows modest, dataset-dependent gains (e.g., only ~3.2% training-time reduction for Burgers) and the paper concedes that optimizing ratios 'remains an exciting future direction,' leaving the practical contribution underdeveloped.

strengths: The paper makes a valuable and timely contribution by critically examining a widely repeated claim (zero-shot super-resolution in FNOs) with a systematic empirical evaluation across three standard PDE datasets (Darcy, Burgers, Navier-Stokes) and multiple resolutions up to 1024.

The decomposition of multi-resolution inference into two orthogonal behaviors—resolution interpolation (varying sampling rate at fixed frequency content) and information extrapolation (varying frequency content at fixed resolution)—is a clear, useful conceptual framing that yields sharper insights than simply reporting aggregate loss numbers.

The spectral (energy spectrum) analysis of model predictions versus ground truth is a well-chosen diagnostic that directly visualizes aliasing, making the failure mode concrete and interpretable (e.g., residual energy exploding above the training low-pass limit).

The evaluation of existing corrective approaches (physics-informed optimization constraints and band-limited learning via CNO/CROP) is thorough and provides a genuine service to the community by showing these do not solve the core out-of-distribution problem; the observation that band-limiting prevents aliasing but also precludes high-frequency prediction is insightful.

The proposed multi-resolution training is simple, practical, and well-profiled: the Pareto analysis of data cost vs. test loss (Fig. 9), memory/training-time savings (Tables 3-4), and demonstration that mostly low-resolution data suffices is an actionable finding for practitioners.

Reproducibility is a clear strength: extensive appendices with hyperparameter grids, model configurations, sensitivity analysis over 3 random seeds, downsampling-strategy ablations, anti-aliasing activation ablations, DeepONet extension, and even hardware-architecture benchmarking across 6 platforms.
The paper is well written with clear figures, and the code release is promised with details sufficient to reproduce experiments.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core finding—that ML models fail to generalize to out-of-distribution discretizations—is not surprising, and much of it is already acknowledged in prior work that the authors themselves cite (e.g., Gao et al. 2025, Lanthaler et al. 2024, Berner et al. 2025, Rowbottom et al. 2025). The paper's contribution is primarily a rigorous negative-result study plus a standard data-mixing remedy, rather than a new method or theory.

Scope of claims vs. evidence: the abstract and title generalize to 'MLOs,' but experiments cover only FNO (main analysis) plus CNO, CROP, and DeepONet in appendices. Other prominent operator families (graph neural operators, transformer-based operators, mesh-invariant architectures) are untested, so the sweeping conclusion that 'MLOs are not able to perform accurate zero-shot multi-resolution inference' is stronger than the evidence.

The multi-resolution training solution is largely an engineering/data-curation remedy: the ratio selection is empirical (grid search over pairwise and all-resolution mixes), and the authors concede that 'optimizing the ratios across all resolutions remains an exciting future direction.' There is no principle or analysis explaining why mostly low-resolution data works, limiting the contribution's depth.

Multi-resolution training data was already explored in prior work (e.g., Li et al. 2024a multi-resolution active learning; several multi-resolution training citations); the paper's novelty here is incremental—an empirical profiling of ratios and costs rather than a new technique.

Some quantitative results complicate the headline narrative: for Darcy and Burgers, sub-resolution losses degrade only by 1-2x, and certain off-resolution cells in Fig. 16 are competitive, suggesting the failure is concentrated in super-resolution and in the turbulent Navier-Stokes regime; the paper could be more nuanced about when zero-shot inference is and is not adequate.

The physics-informed loss comparison (Sec. 4.1) is somewhat unfair in scope: only one formulation of physics constraints from a single prior work is tested with a small weight grid; stronger physics-based training or inference-time projection methods are not considered, yet the conclusion is stated broadly ('physics-informed constraints do not enable multi-resolution generalization').

Evaluation is confined to three PDEBench-style datasets with smooth/turbulent fluid dynamics; generalization of the conclusions to other PDE families, irregular geometries, or adaptive-mesh settings (which motivate the problem in the introduction) is unverified.

Some presentation issues: the abstract's central claim ('we find that MLOs are not able to perform accurate inference...') would benefit from precise scoping; a few appendix figures are low-information-density (e.g., Fig. 32 duplicating Fig. 31), and the code links in the reproducibility statement are placeholders.
